subject: Printable allergy summary & source record review
label: Before you print
headline: What belongs on a personal allergy summary?
summary: A practical guide to reviewing the fields on your summary and understanding what a printed copy cannot establish.
sections: AllergyFolio presents the substance, reaction, severity and verification information supplied in an authorized record. These fields tell different parts of the source entry. A compact summary should preserve those distinctions rather than reduce the entry to a substance name in large type. The app organizes the source information; it does not verify an allergy.

Review each entry and any missing-category or sync warnings before creating a copy. The summary can include recorded medications if that information is useful for your conversation. Adding them does not create an interaction check or establish that the list is current. Questions and corrections should be discussed with the relevant care team or source organization.
An empty list is not a clearance

No returned allergy entries can mean information was unavailable, outside the selected categories or absent from the supplied snapshot. It must not be read as proof of no allergies. AllergyFolio deliberately keeps this limitation visible. A personal printout is not a verified emergency identifier, a clinical certification or a substitute for the medical record.
A copy has its own lifetime

Printing creates a separate copy that will not change when the source is corrected or a session ends. Consider where you keep it and who can see it. Check the available source context again before relying on an older copy for a new conversation. Revoking digital access cannot retrieve paper already printed or remove a downloaded file.

The public site is ready for browsing, and the record workflow requires production activation before live imports are available. You will choose categories before external authorization. The privacy notice explains the current connection and consent details. Its guides remain public and contain no patient records.
guideIntro: Create a readable personal allergy summary, decide whether to include medications, and understand what happens to a printed or saved copy after the session ends.

articles.title: How to print a personal allergy summary with AllergyFolio
articles.description: Review recorded reactions, severity and verification fields, choose whether to include medications, and check the print preview before saving a personal copy.

sections.heading: Review the identity and recorded entries
paragraphs: The summary starts with the name from the authorized record. Check that it is the intended record before making a copy. For each allergy entry, read the label, recorded reaction, source severity, status and verification information. Missing fields are displayed as not supplied.

sections.heading: Decide whether medication names belong on this copy
paragraphs: The optional medication checkbox adds recorded medication names to the summary. It does not turn the page into a full medication review or add detailed directions. Choose the option according to the purpose of the personal copy you are making.
items: Check the displayed identity.
Read every included allergy entry and its source context.
Choose whether to include recorded medication names.
Open the browser print preview and check that the text is readable.

sections.heading: Use the browser’s print controls
paragraphs: “Print my summary” opens the browser print dialog. Paper size, margins, page breaks and saving as PDF are handled there. Inspect the preview before printing or saving, especially when the record contains several entries.

sections.heading: Label the copy for what it is
paragraphs: AllergyFolio produces a personal summary, not a verified emergency ID or a clinical certificate. An empty returned list does not establish that someone has no allergies. The copy does not update itself; compare it with the appropriate current source when you next use it. Live imports remain subject to production activation.

questions.question: Does the medication option include doses?
questions.answer: The optional section lists recorded medication names. It is not a complete directions or prescription report.

questions.question: Can AllergyFolio certify my allergy information?
questions.answer: No. It formats returned source information for personal review and printing.

articles.title: What happens to a printed allergy summary after disconnecting?
articles.description: Understand why ending an AllergyFolio session or revoking a connection does not update or erase paper copies and saved PDFs.

sections.heading: A printout is a separate object
paragraphs: The page on screen is part of a temporary record session. A paper printout or saved PDF is a separate copy created through the browser. Once produced, it does not depend on the session remaining open to be readable.

sections.heading: Disconnecting ends access, not the life of a copy
paragraphs: Ending a local session removes that session’s access in the application. Managing or revoking authorized sharing acts on the connection. Neither action can reach a sheet of paper or automatically remove a file you saved elsewhere.

sections.heading: Keep your copies understandable
paragraphs: Before relying on a saved summary, consider when you created it and whether the source information may have changed. If you replace an old copy, manage the old paper or file yourself. The app does not offer a remote document update or deletion mechanism.

sections.heading: Make a deliberate decision to export
paragraphs: The print control is an explicit action, which gives you a moment to review what will leave the temporary workspace. Use the preview to confirm whether medication names are included and whether the source details remain readable. Avoid placing personal health information in public issue trackers when asking about a formatting problem.

questions.question: Will a saved PDF change when the source record changes?
questions.answer: No. A saved PDF is a snapshot of the page when you printed it.

questions.question: Can the site erase a copy I already printed?
questions.answer: No. Paper and separately saved files are outside the site’s session controls.

articles.title: Why printable health tools still matter in an API-first product
articles.description: AllergyFolio explains how a narrow authorized data connection can support a useful paper or PDF output without turning a personal summary into a certificate.

sections.heading: The final interaction may happen away from a screen
paragraphs: A health product can begin with an API and end with a page someone can hold. A printable summary gives a visitor a deliberate way to carry selected information into another conversation. The design question is what remains understandable when navigation, expandable panels and connection controls are no longer present.
AllergyFolio’s answer is a compact view of supplied allergy details, with optional medication names. The printable page is the product’s output, not merely a screenshot of a larger dashboard.

sections.heading: Preserve the fields that make a label interpretable
paragraphs: An allergy label by itself can conceal important distinctions in the returned record. The layout keeps recorded reaction, source severity, status, verification information and source context together. If a field is absent, the page should still communicate that absence.

Those choices make the copy easier to discuss and inspect. They do not clinically verify the record or establish that an incomplete list is complete. The format should carry the same limitations as the screen it came from.

sections.heading: Use connectivity to support a focused output
paragraphs: The AllergyFolio implementation is powered by FinchNode for the authorized record handoff. Its own interface decides which supplied details appear in the compact layout and whether medication names are included. That is the part of the experience a business can refine for its audience.

A connection layer is valuable here because the product can work from a defined response rather than ask the visitor to retype every field. The current site still requires production activation before it can import live records.

links.label: AllergyFolio’s allowed categories and connection setup

sections.heading: Treat the print preview as a review step
paragraphs: The print action opens the browser’s dialog. Page size, margins and saving to PDF remain browser choices. Make the preview part of the workflow: a user can check identity, included sections and readability before committing the copy.
items: Keep the source and missing-field labels legible.
Avoid a design that implies emergency certification.
Check long entries and multi-page output.
Make optional medication names a deliberate choice.

sections.heading: Separate portability from ongoing access
paragraphs: Once printed or saved, the summary has a separate lifetime. Ending a session does not update the paper, and changing a source record does not rewrite a saved PDF. A good portable output tells the truth about that boundary.

For an independent operator, the opportunity is a simple and well-explained artifact. Additional connectivity should serve that artifact’s purpose, rather than expanding record access without a corresponding benefit to the visitor.

questions.question: Does an API-backed printout become an official medical document?
questions.answer: No. AllergyFolio formats supplied information as a personal summary. Its connection method does not confer clinical certification.

questions.question: Why offer paper when the records are digital?
questions.answer: A portable copy can support a conversation outside the app. Its usefulness depends on clear content, source context and an explanation that it will not update automatically.

articles.title: How to share your allergy list in an emergency: phone, paper and ID options
articles.description: Compare iPhone Medical ID, Android emergency info, signed emergency care plans and medical ID jewelry, and learn how to keep every copy of your allergy list consistent.

sections.heading: One allergy list, several audiences
paragraphs: The people who need your allergy information are rarely the same people who treat you routinely. A paramedic may have your locked phone, a teacher may have a paper plan, and an urgent-care clinic may have only what you can tell them. Each of those settings favors a different format.

This guide compares the common options for making an allergy list available when you cannot explain it yourself. None of them replaces the treatment plan your own clinician gives you; they are ways to make that plan and the underlying allergy list easier to find.

sections.heading: iPhone: Medical ID in the Health app
paragraphs: Apple’s Medical ID lives in the Health app. From the Summary tab, tap your profile picture, then Medical ID, and use Edit to fill in fields including Allergies, Medications and Conditions, along with emergency contacts.

Turning on Show When Locked lets someone open Medical ID from the Lock screen without your passcode. That is the point of the feature, but it also means anything you enter is visible to whoever is holding the phone. Enter what a responder needs, not your whole history.

links.label: Apple: Set up your Medical ID

sections.heading: Android: emergency information in the Safety app
paragraphs: On Android 12 and later, Google’s Safety app (listed as Personal Safety in the Play Store) holds emergency information. Under Your info, the Medical information section has fields for blood type, allergies and medications.

To make the details visible without unlocking, the app’s Emergency info access setting has a Show when locked option. Google notes that anyone who picks up the phone can then see that information, and you can switch the setting off again in the Safety app. Menus vary slightly between phone makers.

links.label: Google: Get help during an emergency with your Android phone

sections.heading: Paper: a signed emergency care plan
paragraphs: For severe allergies, a written emergency plan signed by a clinician is often what schools, camps and workplaces ask for. FARE’s Food Allergy & Anaphylaxis Emergency Care Plan, formerly called the Food Allergy Action Plan, lists allergens, symptoms, treatment steps and emergency contacts in one page. The American Academy of Pediatrics publishes its own Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan.

The value of a paper plan is that it states what to do, not only what you react to. Ask your clinician to complete it, keep copies wherever you spend time, and replace old copies when doses or instructions change.

links.label: AAP Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan (PDF)

sections.heading: Wearable: medical ID jewelry and services
paragraphs: The American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology notes that some people at risk of anaphylaxis wear medical jewelry so others know they have allergies and may need epinephrine. Jewelry works without a battery or a phone and is visible at a glance.

Engraving space is limited, so some services add a phone line or online profile behind the ID. MedicAlert Foundation, a nonprofit founded in 1956, pairs its IDs with a membership that includes a 24/7 emergency response team and stored health information. Compare what a service stores, who can reach it and what it costs before signing up.

paragraphs: Most people with a serious allergy use more than one of these. The table summarizes the trade-offs.

sections.heading: Keep every copy saying the same thing
paragraphs: The riskiest allergy list is two lists that disagree. When an allergy is added, removed or re-described after testing, update each place you keep it on the same day.
items: Start from the allergy list in your clinician’s record or patient portal, and ask for corrections there first.
Record the reaction as well as the allergen, because “rash” and “throat swelling” call for different responses.
Update your phone, the signed plan and any ID service together, then discard old printouts.
Check expiry dates on epinephrine devices at the same time.

questions.question: Can first responders see my Medical ID without my passcode?
questions.answer: Yes, if you turn on Show When Locked on iPhone or Show when locked on Android. That also means anyone else holding the phone can see it.

questions.question: Should I list mild intolerances alongside severe allergies?
questions.answer: That is a question for your clinician. Many people keep emergency formats focused on reactions that need urgent treatment, and keep a fuller list in their medical record.
